claim: GWAS of urate in UK Biobank identified 222 independent genome-wide significant signals.
source: Performing GWAS of urate in the UK Biobank data set, we identified 222 independent genome-wide significant signals, summarized in Figure 1A (further details in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number of independent genome-wide significant signals identified in the urate GWAS.

claim: Six of the 10 most significant signals for urate are located within 100 kb of a urate solute transport gene.
source: Remarkably, six of the 10 most significant signals are located within 100 kb of a urate solute transport gene.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding based on the GWAS results.

claim: Eight out of 10 annotated urate transporters have genome-wide significant signals within 100 kb.
source: A recent review identified 10 genes that are involved in urate solute transport in the kidneys (Wright et al., 2010; Anzai et al., 2007); in addition to the six transporters with extremely strong signals, two additional transporters have weaker, yet still genome-wide significant signals (Figure 1B). Hence, GWAS highlights eight out of 10 annotated urate transporters, although some transporters were originally identified using early GWAS for urate levels.
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of urate transporters with GWAS hits and cites prior reviews identifying these transporters.

claim: SMCT1 and SMCT2 do not have GWAS hits for urate levels.
source: The two genes in the pathway that do not have hits (SMCT1 and SMCT2; also known as SLC5A8 and SLC5A12) do not directly transport urate, but instead transport monocarboxylate substrates for URAT1 to increase reabsorption rate (Bobulescu and Moe, 2012) and thus may be less direct regulators of urate levels.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly identifies these two genes as lacking GWAS hits and cites a reference explaining their indirect role.

claim: Five of the top hits for urate are close to transcription factors involved in kidney and liver development.
source: Among the other top hits, five are close to transcription factors involved in kidney and liver development (HNF4G, HNF1A, HNF4A, HLF, and MAF).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly lists these transcription factors as being near top GWAS hits.

claim: The associated missense variant in HNF4A results in differential regulation of the urate solute carrier ABCG2.
source: These are not part of a globally enriched gene set, but recent functional work has shown that the associated missense variant in HNF4A results in differential regulation of the urate solute carrier ABCG2 (Tin et al., 2019), while the MAF association has been shown to regulate SLC5A8 (Leask et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study demonstrating this functional relationship.

claim: The MAF association has been shown to regulate SLC5A8.
source: These are not part of a globally enriched gene set, but recent functional work has shown that the associated missense variant in HNF4A results in differential regulation of the urate solute carrier ABCG2 (Tin et al., 2019), while the MAF association has been shown to regulate SLC5A8 (Leask et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study demonstrating this regulatory relationship.

claim: Serum urate SNP-based heritability was most-highly enriched in kidney regulatory regions (29-fold compared to the genome-wide average SNP, p=1.9e-13).
source: Serum urate SNP-based heritability was most-highly enriched in kidney regulatory regions (29-fold compared to the genome-wide average SNP, p=1.9e-13), while other cell types were enriched around 8-fold (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; see also Tin et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript reports the enrichment value and p-value from stratified LD Score regression analysis.

claim: When active kidney regions were removed from regulatory annotations for other tissues, this eliminated most of the signal found in other cell types for urate heritability.
source: We hypothesized that the enrichment for other tissues might be driven by elements shared between kidney and other cell types. Indeed, when we removed active kidney regions from the regulatory annotations for other tissues, this eliminated most of the signal found in other cell types (Figure 1C).
evidence: The manuscript describes the result of this analysis and references the figure showing the results.

claim: Most serum urate heritability is driven by kidney regulatory variation.
source: Thus, our analysis supports the inference that most serum urate heritability is driven by kidney regulatory variation.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the tissue enrichment analysis.

claim: Genes in the urate metabolic pathway show a modest enrichment for GWAS hits relative to all annotated, protein coding genes (2.1-fold, p=0.017).
source: Overall, we found that genes in the urate metabolic pathway show a modest enrichment for GWAS hits relative to all annotated, protein coding genes as a background (2.1-fold, p=0.017; Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript reports the enrichment value and p-value from the pathway analysis.

claim: XDH, which catalyzes the last step of urate synthesis, has an adjacent GWAS hit.
source: XDH, which catalyzes the last step of urate synthesis, has an adjacent GWAS hit, as do a number of upstream regulators of urate synthesis.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation from the GWAS results.

claim: The overall level of signal in the urate synthesis pathway is modest compared to that seen for kidney urate transporters.
source: Nonetheless, the overall level of signal in the synthesis pathway is modest compared to that seen for kidney urate transporters, suggesting that synthesis, while it plays a role in common variation in urate levels, is secondary to the secretion pathway.
evidence: The manuscript compares the strength of signals between the synthesis and transport pathways.

claim: GWAS of serum IGF-1 levels in 317,000 unrelated White British individuals found a total of 354 distinct association signals at genome-wide significance.
source: In our GWAS of serum IGF-1 levels in 317,000 unrelated White British individuals, we found a total of 354 distinct association signals at genome-wide significance (Figure 3, further details in Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number of significant signals identified in the IGF-1 GWAS.

claim: Eight of the most significant signals for IGF-1 are key parts of the IGF-1 pathway.
source: Eight of the most significant signals are key parts of the IGF-1 pathway (Figure 4).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding and references the figure showing the pathway.

claim: The top hit for IGF-1 is an intergenic SNP between IGFBP3 and another gene, TNS3 (p=1e-837).
source: The top hit is an intergenic SNP between IGFBP3 and another gene, TNS3 (Supplementary file 2; p=1e-837).
evidence: The manuscript reports the top hit and its p-value.

claim: IGFBP3 encodes the main transport protein for IGF-1 and IGF-2 in the bloodstream.
source: IGFBP3 encodes the main transport protein for IGF-1 and IGF-2 in the bloodstream (Firth and Baxter, 2002).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference describing the function of IGFBP3.

claim: IGFALS is an IGFBP cofactor that also binds IGF-1 in serum.
source: Two other lead hits are associated with the IGF transport complex IGFBP: IGFALS, which is an IGFBP cofactor that also binds IGF-1 in serum (Baxter et al., 1989), and PAPPA2, a protease which cleaves and negatively regulates IGFBPs (Overgaard et al., 2001).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference describing the function of IGFALS.

claim: PAPPA2 is a protease which cleaves and negatively regulates IGFBPs.
source: Two other lead hits are associated with the IGF transport complex IGFBP: IGFALS, which is an IGFBP cofactor that also binds IGF-1 in serum (Baxter et al., 1989), and PAPPA2, a protease which cleaves and negatively regulates IGFBPs (Overgaard et al., 2001).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference describing the function of PAPPA2.

claim: GHSR is a pituitary-expressed receptor for the signaling protein ghrelin which negatively regulates the growth hormone (GH) signaling pathway upstream of IGF-1.
source: Three other lead hits lie elsewhere in the growth hormone–IGF axis: GHSR is a pituitary-expressed receptor for the signaling protein ghrelin which negatively regulates the growth hormone (GH) signaling pathway upstream of IGF-1 (Laron, 2001); and FOXO3 and RIN2 lie in downstream signaling pathways (Stitt et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference describing the function of GHSR.

claim: FOXO3 and RIN2 lie in downstream signaling pathways of IGF-1.
source: Three other lead hits lie elsewhere in the growth hormone–IGF axis: GHSR is a pituitary-expressed receptor for the signaling protein ghrelin which negatively regulates the growth hormone (GH) signaling pathway upstream of IGF-1 (Laron, 2001); and FOXO3 and RIN2 lie in downstream signaling pathways (Stitt et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference describing the roles of FOXO3 and RIN2.

claim: The growth hormone secretion pathway shows strong enrichment of GWAS signals (14 out of 32 genes within 100 kb of a genome-wide significant signal, 7.3-fold enrichment, Fisher's exact p=5.4e-7).
source: The first pathway regulates growth hormone secretion, acting in the pituitary to integrate ghrelin and growth hormone releasing hormone signals and produce growth hormone. This pathway shows strong enrichment, with 14 out of 32 genes within 100 kb of a genome-wide significant signal (7.3-fold enrichment, Fisher's exact p=5.4e-7).
evidence: The manuscript reports the enrichment statistics for this pathway.

claim: The IGF-1 secretion pathway shows very strong enrichment of GWAS signals (10/14 genes, 23-fold enrichment, p=4.9e-8).
source: The second pathway, IGF-1 secretion, acts in the liver, where growth hormone triggers JAK-STAT signaling, leading to IGF-1 production and secretion (Dehkhoda et al., 2018). This pathway again shows very strong enrichment of GWAS signals (10/14 genes, 23-fold enrichment, p=4.9e-8).
evidence: The manuscript reports the enrichment statistics for this pathway.

claim: The serum balance of IGF pathway shows strong enrichment of GWAS signals (10/18 genes, 11.7-fold enrichment, p=1.5e-6).
source: The third pathway, serum balance of IGF, relates to IGF-1 itself, and its paralogs, as well as other binding partners and their regulators in the serum. Here 10/18 genes have GWAS hits (11.7-fold enrichment, p=1.5e-6).
evidence: The manuscript reports the enrichment statistics for this pathway.

claim: Many of the genes in the AKT branch of the IGF-1 signaling cascade were close to a genome-wide significant association (9/31 genes; 3.8-fold enrichment, p=0.002).
source: Most notably, many of the genes in the AKT branch of the IGF-1 signaling cascade were close to a genome-wide significant association including FOXO3 (9/31 genes; 3.8-fold enrichment, p=0.002).
evidence: The manuscript reports the enrichment statistics for this pathway.

claim: The RAB/MAPK/RAS pathway was not enriched overall for IGF-1 GWAS hits (p=0.59).
source: In contrast, the RAB/MAPK/RAS pathway was not enriched overall (p=0.59), although one key signaling molecule (RIN2) in this pathway was located at one of the strongest hits genome-wide.
evidence: The manuscript reports the lack of enrichment for this pathway.

claim: No signal of epistasis was found among the 77 most significant (p<1e-20) lead SNPs for IGF-1.
source: We found no signal of epistasis among the 77 most significant (p<1e-20) lead SNPs for IGF-1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), and weak enrichment of signal among the top 38 urate lead SNPs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2 inset; see Materials and methods).
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of the epistasis analysis.

claim: IGF-1 lead SNPs (p<5e-8) showed weak, global inflation of test statistics for departures from additivity.
source: Similarly, IGF-1 lead SNPs (p<5e-8) showed weak, global inflation of test statistics for departures from additivity (e.g. domininance or recessivity) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), while the two most significant urate hits showed significant minor dominant (SLC2A9) and minor recessive (ABCG2) effects that were nevertheless substantially smaller than the additive effects (Figure 3—figure supplement 3 inset).
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of the non-additivity analysis.

claim: The two most significant urate hits showed significant minor dominant (SLC2A9) and minor recessive (ABCG2) effects that were nevertheless substantially smaller than the additive effects.
source: Similarly, IGF-1 lead SNPs (p<5e-8) showed weak, global inflation of test statistics for departures from additivity (e.g. domininance or recessivity) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), while the two most significant urate hits showed significant minor dominant (SLC2A9) and minor recessive (ABCG2) effects that were nevertheless substantially smaller than the additive effects (Figure 3—figure supplement 3 inset).
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of the non-additivity analysis for urate.

claim: Non-linear genotype effects, while likely present to some degree, are substantially weaker than additive components, even when the strongest effects are concentrated in the same biological pathways.
source: Building upon previous studies (Wei et al., 2014; Zaitlen et al., 2013) that have found little evidence of epistasis or dominance in human populations, these results indicate that non-linear genotype effects, while likely present to some degree, are substantially weaker than additive components, even when the strongest effects are concentrated in the same biological pathways and would thus be more likely to show epistasis.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the epistasis and non-additivity analyses, citing previous studies.

claim: Testosterone is synthesized from cholesterol as one possible product of the steroid biosynthesis pathway.
source: Testosterone is synthesized from cholesterol as one possible product of the steroid biosynthesis pathway.
evidence: The manuscript states this as established biological knowledge.

claim: Testosterone synthesis occurs primarily in the testis in males, and in the ovary and adrenal glands in females.
source: Synthesis occurs primarily in the testis in males, and in the ovary and adrenal glands in females.
evidence: The manuscript states this as established biological knowledge.

claim: Testosterone production is stimulated by the hypothalmic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis.
source: Testosterone production is stimulated by the hypothalmic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis: gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) signals from the hypothalamus to the pituitary to cause production and secretion of luteinizing hormone (LH); LH in turn signals to the gonads to produce testosterone.
evidence: The manuscript describes this as established biological knowledge.

claim: The HPG axis is subject to a negative feedback loop as testosterone inhibits production of GnRH and LH by the hypothalamus and pituitary.
source: The HPG axis is subject to a negative feedback loop as testosterone inhibits production of GnRH and LH by the hypothalamus and pituitary to ensure tight control of testosterone levels (Javorsky et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference describing this feedback mechanism.

claim: Approximately half of the circulating testosterone (∼40% in males, ∼60% in females) is bound to sex hormone binding globulin (SHBG) and is generally considered non-bioavailable.
source: Approximately half of the circulating testosterone (∼40% in males, ∼60% in females [Dunn et al., 1981]) is bound to sex hormone binding globulin (SHBG) and is generally considered non-bioavailable.
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference for these percentages.

claim: Testosterone breakdown occurs primarily in the liver in both females and males.
source: Testosterone breakdown occurs primarily in the liver in both females and males.
evidence: The manuscript states this as established biological knowledge.

claim: Testosterone shows minimal genetic correlation between the sexes.
source: In our preliminary analysis, we found that testosterone shows minimal genetic correlation between the sexes, in contrast to other biomarkers including urate and IGF-1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports this finding from genetic correlation analysis.

claim: GWAS of testosterone in UKBB females (N = 142,778) discovered 79 independent genome-wide significant signals.
source: Here, we performed testosterone GWAS in UKBB females (N = 142,778) and males (N = 146,339) separately. We discovered 79 and 127 independent genome-wide significant signals in females and males, respectively (Figure 5, further details in Supplementary file 3–4).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number of significant signals identified in the female testosterone GWAS.

claim: GWAS of testosterone in UKBB males (N = 146,339) discovered 127 independent genome-wide significant signals.
source: Here, we performed testosterone GWAS in UKBB females (N = 142,778) and males (N = 146,339) separately. We discovered 79 and 127 independent genome-wide significant signals in females and males, respectively (Figure 5, further details in Supplementary file 3–4).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number of significant signals identified in the male testosterone GWAS.

claim: In females, six of the most significant signals for testosterone are close to genes involved in testosterone biosythesis.
source: In females, six of the most significant signals are close to genes involved in testosterone biosythesis (Figure 5A); together these results suggest that the steroid biosynthesis pathway is the primary controller of female testosterone levels.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding from the female testosterone GWAS.

claim: The top hit for female testosterone is at a locus containing three genes involved in hydroxylation of testosterone and estrone, CYP3A4, CYP3A5, and CYP3A7.
source: Among these, the top hit is at a locus containing three genes involved in hydroxylation of testosterone and estrone, CYP3A4, CYP3A5, and CYP3A7 (Kandel et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2003; Kuehl et al., 2001).
evidence: The manuscript cites references describing the functions of these genes.

claim: Two other lead hits for female testosterone (MCM9 and FGF9) are involved in gonad development.
source: Two other lead hits (MCM9 and FGF9) are involved in gonad development (Lutzmann et al., 2012; Wood-Trageser et al., 2014; Colvin et al., 2001).
evidence: The manuscript cites references describing the roles of these genes in gonad development.

claim: The lead hits in males for testosterone are largely non-overlapping with those from females.
source: Strikingly, and in agreement with recent studies and in agreement with recent studies (Flynn et al., 2021; Ruth et al., 2020), the lead hits in males are largely non-overlapping with those from females.
evidence: The manuscript states this observation and cites recent studies with similar findings.

claim: Three of the most significant signals for male testosterone affect the steroid biosynthesis pathway (SRD5A2, UGT2B15, and AKR1C).
source: Three of the most significant signals affect the steroid biosynthesis pathway (SRD5A2, UGT2B15, and AKR1C); three are involved in either upstream activation (NR0B2) (Vega et al., 2015) or downstream signaling (the androgen receptor, AR, and its co-chaperone FKBP4), respectively; and two have been implicated in the development of the GnRH-releasing function of the hypothalamus (KAL1) (Franco et al., 1991) or the gonads (NR2F2) (Qin et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly lists these genes and their roles.

claim: The largest category of male testosterone hits is for a group of eight distinct variants previously shown to affect sex hormone binding globulin (SHBG) levels.
source: However, the largest category, including the most significant hit overall, is for a group of eight distinct variants previously shown to affect sex hormone binding globulin (SHBG) levels (Coviello et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference identifying these SHBG-associated variants.

claim: Nearly all major steps of the steroid hormone biosynthesis pathway contained a gene near a genome-wide significant SNP in either females or males: 31 out of 61 genes are within 100 kb of a genome-wide significant signal.
source: We observed that nearly all major steps of the pathway contained a gene near a genome-wide significant SNP in either females or males: 31 out of 61 genes are within 100 kb of a genome-wide significant signal in males, females or both.
evidence: The manuscript reports this finding from the pathway analysis.

claim: The KEGG steroid hormone pathway shows strong enrichment for signals in both females and males (26-fold enrichment, p=2.5e-8 in females; 11-fold enrichment, p=1.2e-4 in males).
source: Indeed, the KEGG steroid hormone pathway shows strong enrichment for signals in both females and males (26-fold enrichment, p=2.5e-8 in females; 11-fold enrichment, p=1.2e-4 in males; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the enrichment statistics for this pathway.

claim: Male hits and female hits tend to occur in different parts of the steroid hormone biosynthesis pathway.
source: More broadly, male hits and female hits tend to occur in different parts of the steroid hormone biosynthesis pathway: catalytic steps involved in progestagen and corticosteroid synthesis and metabolism only showed hits in females, while most male hits were concentrated within androgen synthesis, either upstream or downstream of testosterone itself (Figure 6).
evidence: The manuscript describes this pattern observed in the pathway analysis.

claim: There is no correlation in the effect sizes among lead SNPs for testosterone between females and males.
source: This is true for genome-wide significant hits, for which there is no correlation in the effect sizes among lead SNPs (Figure 7A), as well as genome-wide, as the global genetic correlation between females and males is approximately zero (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports this finding from the genetic correlation analysis.

claim: The global genetic correlation between female and male testosterone is approximately zero.
source: This is true for genome-wide significant hits, for which there is no correlation in the effect sizes among lead SNPs (Figure 7A), as well as genome-wide, as the global genetic correlation between females and males is approximately zero (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports this finding from the genetic correlation analysis.

claim: The HPG axis plays a more significant role in regulating testosterone production in males than in females.
source: As we show below, two aspects of testosterone biology can explain these extreme sex differences in genetic architecture. First, the hypothalmic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis plays a more significant role in regulating testosterone production in males than in females.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a conclusion from the analyses presented.

claim: SHBG plays an important role in mediating the negative feedback portion of the HPG axis in males but not in females.
source: Second, SHBG plays an important role in mediating the negative feedback portion of the HPG axis in males but not in females.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a conclusion from the analyses presented.

claim: Hits for both male testosterone and male CBAT were found throughout the HPG signaling cascade.
source: We found hits for both male testosterone and male CBAT throughout the HPG signaling cascade (Figure 7B).
evidence: The manuscript reports this finding from the GWAS results.

claim: All HPG signaling hits showed more significant effects on CBAT as compared to total testosterone.
source: All these hits showed more significant effects on CBAT as compared to total testosterone (Figure 7—figure supplement 3), suggesting that their primary role is in regulating bioavailable testosterone.
evidence: The manuscript reports this finding from the GWAS comparison.

claim: HPG signaling hits do not show signals in females.
source: Importantly, these HPG signaling hits do not show signals in females.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation.

claim: The adrenal gland produces ∼50% of serum testosterone in females.
source: First, the adrenal gland, which is not subject to control by HPG signaling, produces ∼50% of serum testosterone in females.
evidence: The manuscript states this as established biological knowledge.

claim: GWAS hits for female testosterone cluster in steroid hormone pathways involving progestagen and corticosteroid synthesis.
source: Consistent with this idea, GWAS hits for female testosterone cluster in steroid hormone pathways involving progestagen and corticosteroid synthesis (Figure 6), processes known to occur largely in the adrenal.
evidence: The manuscript reports this finding from the pathway analysis.

claim: Female testosterone hits are specifically enriched for high expression in the adrenal gland relative to male testosterone hits.
source: Female testosterone hits are also specifically enriched for high expression in the adrenal gland relative to male testosterone hits (Figure 7—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports this finding from the expression analysis.

claim: The pituitary also secretes follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), which in females stimulates aromatization of androgens (including testosterone) into estrogens.
source: This is because the pituitary also secretes follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), which in females stimulates aromatization of androgens (including testosterone) into estrogens (Ulloa-Aguirre and Michael Conn, 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference describing this biological process.

claim: In males, FSH does not stimulate androgen aromatization but is instead required for sperm production.
source: In males, FSH does not stimulate androgen aromatization but is instead required for sperm production.
evidence: The manuscript states this as established biological knowledge.

claim: A previously described GWAS hit for menstrual cycle length at FSHB shows suggestive association with testosterone in females but not males.
source: Consistent with differential roles of FSH, a previously described GWAS hit for menstrual cycle length at FSHB (Laisk et al., 2018) shows suggestive association with testosterone in females but not males (Supplementary file 6).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference and reports this finding.

claim: There is high positive genetic correlation between female and male SHBG.
source: We found high positive genetic correlation between female and male SHBG, as well as between SHBG and total testosterone in males but not females (Figure 7C).
evidence: The manuscript reports this finding from the genetic correlation analysis.

claim: There is high positive genetic correlation between SHBG and total testosterone in males but not females.
source: We found high positive genetic correlation between female and male SHBG, as well as between SHBG and total testosterone in males but not females (Figure 7C).
evidence: The manuscript reports this finding from the genetic correlation analysis.

claim: There is a significant negative genetic correlation between SHBG and CBAT in both females and males, but of a far larger magnitude in females than males.
source: Additionally, we found a significant negative genetic correlation between SHBG and CBAT in both females and males, but of a far larger magnitude in females than males (Figure 7C).
evidence: The manuscript reports this finding from the genetic correlation analysis.

claim: Increased SHBG leads to decreased bioavailable testosterone in both females and males, and in males this relieves the negative feedback from testosterone on the hypothalamus and pituitary gland, ultimately allowing LH production and increased testosterone production.
source: Combining these observations, we propose that increased SHBG leads to decreased bioavailable testosterone in both females and males, and in males this relieves the negative feedback from testosterone on the hypothalamus and pituitary gland, ultimately allowing LH production and increased testosterone production (Figure 7D).
evidence: The manuscript proposes this model based on the genetic correlation findings.

claim: The lack of SHBG-mediated negative feedback in females is likely due in part to the overall weaker action of the HPG axis, as well as the fact that female testosterone levels are too low to effectively inhibit the HPG axis.
source: The lack of SHBG-mediated negative feedback in females is likely due in part to the overall weaker action of the HPG axis, as well as the fact that female testosterone levels are too low to effectively inhibit the HPG axis.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this explanation based on the findings.

claim: Experimental manipulations of female testosterone result in significant reductions of LH only when increasing testosterone levels to within the range typically found in males.
source: This idea is supported experimental manipulations of female testosterone, which result in significant reductions of LH only when increasing testosterone levels to within the range typically found in males (Serafini et al., 1986).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference describing experimental evidence.

claim: The SLC2A9 locus is responsible for 20% of the SNP-based heritability for urate.
source: In aggregate, core genes contribute modest fractions of SNP-based heritability, with the exception of the SLC2A9 locus, which HESS estimates is responsible for 20% of the SNP-based heritability for urate.
evidence: The manuscript reports this estimate from the HESS analysis.

claim: Aside from the SLC2A9 locus, the core pathways contribute between approximately 1–11 percent of the SNP-based heritability.
source: Aside from this outlier gene, the core pathways contribute between approximately 1–11 percent of the SNP-based heritability.
evidence: The manuscript reports this finding from the heritability analysis.

claim: Around 45–50% of SNPs are linked to a non-zero effect variant for urate, IGF-1 and male testosterone.
source: Overall we estimate that around 45–50% of SNPs are linked to a non-zero effect variant for urate, IGF-1 and male testosterone, and 30% for female testosterone (Figure 8B).
evidence: The manuscript reports these estimates from the ashR analysis.

claim: Around 30% of SNPs are linked to a non-zero effect variant for female testosterone.
source: Overall we estimate that around 45–50% of SNPs are linked to a non-zero effect variant for urate, IGF-1 and male testosterone, and 30% for female testosterone (Figure 8B).
evidence: The manuscript reports this estimate from the ashR analysis.

claim: The estimates of causal variant fractions range from 0.1% of all 4.4M variants with MAF >1% in female and male testosterone (∼4000 causal sites) to 0.3% of variants for urate (∼12,000 causal sites).
source: Overall, our estimates range from 0.1% of all 4.4M variants with MAF >1% in female and male testosterone (∼4000 causal sites) to 0.3% of variants for urate (∼12,000 causal sites).
evidence: The manuscript reports these estimates from the simulation-matching analysis.

claim: For height, the estimate is 2%, or 80,000 causal sites in UK Biobank.
source: These results imply that all four traits are highly polygenic, though considerably less so than height (for which we estimate 2%, or 80,000 causal sites in UK Biobank; Figure 8—figure supplements 2 and 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports this estimate from the simulation-matching analysis.

claim: Causal variants are likely to be clumped in the genome instead of being uniformly distributed; simulations with clumping require a larger number of causal variants to match the data.
source: First, causal variants are likely to be clumped in the genome instead of being uniformly distributed; simulations with clumping require a larger number of causal variants to match the data (Figure 8—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The manuscript reports this finding from sensitivity analyses.

claim: If the distribution of effect sizes has more weight near zero and fatter tails than a normal distribution, this would imply a larger number of causal variants.
source: Second, if the distribution of effect sizes has more weight near zero and fatter tails than a normal distribution, this would imply a larger number of causal variants (see analysis assuming a T-distribution, Figure 8—figure supplement 6).
evidence: The manuscript reports this finding from sensitivity analyses.

claim: Stratified LD Score analysis of the data suggests that some of the apparent evidence for overinflation of the test statistics may in fact be due to a higher proportion of causal variants occurring in lower LD Score bins rather than population stratification.
source: Third, stratified LD Score analysis of the data suggests that some of the apparent evidence for overinflation of the test statistics (Supplementary file 11) may in fact be due to a higher proportion of causal variants occurring in lower LD Score bins (Gazal et al., 2017) rather than population stratification, as the annotation-adjusted intercepts for all traits but height are consistent with 1 (no population stratification).
evidence: The manuscript reports this finding from the stratified LD Score analysis and cites a reference.

claim: GENESIS estimates for the molecular traits assuming a single normal distribution were: male testosterone 0.1%; female testosterone 0.2%; urate 0.3%; IGF-1 0.4%.
source: As an alternative approach, we used the program GENESIS, which uses a likelihood model to fit a mixture of effect sizes using 1–2 normal components, and a null component (Zhang et al., 2018; Supplementary file 12). Assuming a single normal distribution, the results for the molecular traits were very similar to our results: male testosterone 0.1%; female testosterone 0.2%; urate 0.3%; IGF-1 0.4%.
evidence: The manuscript reports these estimates from the GENESIS analysis.

claim: GENESIS estimates for the molecular traits assuming a mixture of two normal distributions were: male testosterone 0.6%; female testosterone 0.7%; urate 1.1%; IGF-1 1.1%.
source: The GENESIS results for a mixture of two normal distributions resulted in a significantly higher overall likelihood, and estimates roughly threefold higher than our estimates: male testosterone 0.6%; female testosterone 0.7%; urate 1.1%; IGF-1 1.1%.
evidence: The manuscript reports these estimates from the GENESIS analysis.

claim: For these molecular traits, around 10–15% of the SNP-based heritability is due to variants in core pathways.
source: In summary this analysis indicates that for these molecular traits, around 10–15% of the SNP-based heritability is due to variants in core pathways (and in the case of urate, SLC2A9 is a major outlier, contributing 20% on its own).
evidence: The manuscript summarizes this finding from the heritability analysis.

claim: Most of the SNP-based heritability for these molecular traits is due to a much larger number of variants spread widely across the genome, conservatively estimated at 4000–12,000 common variants for the biomarkers and 80,000 for height.
source: However, most of the SNP-based heritability is due to a much larger number of variants spread widely across the genome, conservatively estimated at 4000–12,000 common variants for the biomarkers and 80,000 for height.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes this finding from the causal variant estimation analysis.

claim: For urate, IGF-1, and testosterone, the top hits are generally close to genes with known biological relevance to the trait in question.
source: As described in more detail below, we performed GWAS for each of these traits in around 300,000 white British individuals from the UK Biobank (Bycroft et al., 2018). For all three traits many of the most significant hits are highly interpretable–a marked difference from GWAS of typical disease traits.
